# Getting On The Net
This guide covers the basic steps needed to use a field headset and set up an AN/PRC-117G manpack radio.
## 1. Check Your Equipment
Most roles use a [bold]field headset[/bold] in the ears slot. CLF personnel use a concealable earpiece instead. Both provide access to the radio nets built into the device.
Some roles also carry an [bold]AN/PRC-117G[/bold] in the back slot. The manpack provides local coverage for relay-gated nets and can carry nets that are not available on a normal headset.
Examine your headset to see which channel prefixes it supports. See [textlink="Field Headsets" link="AU14CommsHeadsets"] for headset-specific controls.
## 2. Radio Coverage
Combat nets are [bold]relay-gated[/bold]. A headset only works when it is within range of equipment carrying that net.
Coverage may come from:
- A powered AN/PRC worn by a trained operator. - A deployed retransmission station. - A command-post antenna mast. - A powered communications array. - A vehicle radio. - A field antenna mast. - CLF base stations, relay sets, or feeder taps where applicable.
If no suitable relay is in range, the combat net cannot be used.
Colony and civilian channels are not relay-gated and continue to work without field radio infrastructure.
Exact ranges are listed in [textlink="Comms Quick Reference" link="AU14CommsQuickRef"].
### Raising a field mast
A field antenna mast is a construction project, not a quick build. It requires [bold]engineering training[/bold] at every step, and a half-built mast carries no nets at all.
From metal sheets, under [bold]antenna mast parts[/bold], build:
- A [bold]mast footing[/bold], placed where the mast is to stand. - A [bold]mast antenna head[/bold], which occupies both hands and must be carried to the site.
Then work the footing up, one interaction at a time:
1. Stake the footing down with a [bold]wrench[/bold]. 2. Bolt up the lattice with [bold]30 metal rods[/bold]. 3. Weld the joints with a [bold]blowtorch[/bold]. 4. Run the guys and feeder with [bold]15 cable[/bold]. 5. Fit the [bold]mast antenna head[/bold]. 6. Pack the feed with [bold]10 plasteel[/bold], then tune it with an [bold]access tuner[/bold].
Examine the work in progress at any point to see the step it is waiting on. An unfinished mast can be pried apart for part of its metal back, and a finished one can be dismantled with wirecutters and a wrench.
## 3. Use Your Headset
With a headset worn, use its channel prefix followed by your message.
The default headset channel uses:
[color=#a4885c]:h Radio check, over.[/color]
Other keyed channels use their own prefixes, such as [color=#a4885c]:v[/color] or [color=#a4885c]:a[/color]. Examine the headset to see which channels it carries.
A headset cannot use a faction net for which it has no key. Those keys cannot be added in the field.
Radio traffic shows the sender's callsign rather than their character name. Face-to-face speech is unchanged.
## 4. Open the AN/PRC Panel
AN/PRC controls require radio training.
[bold]GOVFOR and OPFOR[/bold] trained roles include Commander, Adjutant, staff officers, engineering officers, intelligence officers, synthetics, squad leaders, Fireteam Leaders, and Radio Traffic Operators.
[bold]CLF[/bold] trained roles are the Cell Leader and Radio Operator.
A [bold]field radio operator's pamphlet[/bold] permanently grants radio training regardless of role.
To open the set:
- Alt-click the radio or open its verb menu. - Select [bold]Open Radio Panel[/bold].
Everything on the panel is worked from the display: [bold]PRE[/bold] moves the cursor down the lines, [bold]ENT[/bold] works the line under it, [bold]CLR[/bold] backs out, and the soft keys under the glass change screen. Clicking a line moves the cursor to it; clicking it again works it. - Press [bold]6 PWR[/bold], or move the function switch to [bold]CT[/bold] or [bold]PT[/bold].
A powered radio can be programmed while held or lying on the ground. It only needs to be worn or deployed when it must transmit, relay, search, run a radio check, or print its log.
### BIT status
The [bold]BIT[/bold] field shows why a set is not ready:
- [bold]PASS[/bold] — powered, deployed, and on a working memory. - [bold]NO CELL[/bold] — no battery is fitted. - [bold]OFF[/bold] — the set is switched off. - [bold]STOWED[/bold] — powered and programmable, but not worn or deployed. - [bold]NO NET[/bold] — no working memory is selected. - [bold]SRCH[/bold] — the search receiver is active.
## 5. Load a Net
A fresh AN/PRC can store up to [bold]four[/bold] memories.
To add a named net:
- Open [bold]PGM[/bold]. - Move the cursor with [bold]PRE[/bold] to [bold]ADD NET[/bold] and press [bold]ENT[/bold]. - Enter a short label if desired. - Press [bold]ENT[/bold] on the new memory to open it. - Choose [bold]TUNE TO A NET[/bold] and pick the net from the list. - Back out with [bold]CLR[/bold] and choose [bold]WORK THIS NET[/bold]. - Select the memory row to make it active.
The active memory is the one used by [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] and by the handset.
A raw frequency can be entered with [bold]KEY A FREQUENCY[/bold] on the same screen. The display uses an [bold]___.___[/bold] template; [bold]CLR[/bold] removes the last digit and [bold]ENT[/bold] confirms the frequency.
[bold]EMPTY THE MEMORY[/bold] clears a memory while keeping its label. [bold]DELETE THE MEMORY[/bold] removes it entirely.
## 6. Load COMSEC
Secured faction nets require a matching physical fill card in the AN/PRC.
Insert the issued fill card and check the SEC page. A matching current card shows [bold]SECURED[/bold].
If the radio transmits on a secured net without matching fill, it warns the operator and sends the message in the clear.
## 7. Wear or Deploy the Radio
To place the set on the air:
- Wear it in the [bold]back slot[/bold], or - Deploy it with [bold]Set Up Retrans[/bold].
Once deployed and on a working memory, [bold]BIT[/bold] should read [bold]PASS[/bold].
## 8. Transmit Through the AN/PRC
Use [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] to transmit through the active memory:
[color=#a4885c]:r HAVOC 6, this is SABRE ROMEO, radio check, over.[/color]
A worn radio uses the wearer's assigned callsign by default. If no callsign is assigned, the transmission appears as [bold]UNKNOWN STATION[/bold].
Press [bold]ENT[/bold] on [bold]RADIO CHECK[/bold] on the OPT screen, or press [bold]1 CALL[/bold], to test coverage on the active net. The radio sends [bold]RADIO CHECK, HOW COPY, OVER[/bold] and returns a private list of stations in clear or degraded coverage.
## The Handset
The handset allows a nearby character to use the AN/PRC's active memory without radio training.
To take it:
- Stand within cord range of the wearer or deployed radio. - Keep one hand free. - Alt-click the wearer or radio. - Select [bold]Take Handset[/bold].
While the handset is held, normal spoken speech is transmitted over the radio's active memory. Whispered speech is not transmitted.
The handset uses the holder's callsign. Only one person can hold it at a time, and it disconnects when the holder moves out of range. Use [bold]Hang Up Handset[/bold] to return it.
If the handset user is already wearing another AN/PRC, their own pack takes priority and normal [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] operation is used instead.
## CLF Coverage
The CLF do not have a fixed communications array. Their combat nets rely on portable or improvised infrastructure.
CLF coverage can be provided by:
- A worn AN/PRC. - A clandestine base station. - A staked-down relay set. - A field antenna mast. - A feeder tap installed on a compatible mast or array.
The issued CLF manpack starts with [bold]CLF[/bold] and [bold]CLF Command[/bold] already loaded as [bold]CELL[/bold] and [bold]CMD[/bold].
### Feeder taps
A CLF Radio Operator can use a [bold]net splice kit[/bold] on a compatible mast or array. A successful splice adds CLF nets to that infrastructure without disabling its existing nets.
The splice panel is operated by probing the band for hidden carriers and locking each carrier once its position is known. Failed locks consume additional probes and increase detection. Running out of probes or filling the detection meter fails the attempt and faults the junction temporarily.
Installed taps are visible, can be removed, and contain a keying module that can be recovered by whoever removes them.
Exact splice values are listed in [textlink="Comms Quick Reference" link="AU14CommsQuickRef"].
## Troubleshooting
[bold]Problem[/bold] [bold]Check[/bold]
No traffic on a combat net Check that a relay carrying the net is in range.
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] uses the wrong net Select the correct active memory on PGM.
The radio panel will not open The character does not have radio training.
The panel is unresponsive Check power and battery state. [bold]NO CELL[/bold] means no battery is fitted.
RADIO CHECK, SEARCH, or PRINT is unavailable Check BIT. [bold]STOWED[/bold] means the set must be worn or deployed first.
LD or Z returns to another position Normal operation. LD and Z are momentary detents.
Traffic is broken or static-filled The signal is weak, degraded, jammed, or cannot be decoded.
Secured AN/PRC traffic is static Check that both sides have compatible current COMSEC fill.
A headset channel is missing Examine the headset. Missing faction keys cannot be added in the field.
Transmission shows UNKNOWN STATION No callsign is assigned to the sender or fixed station.
Normal speech is being transmitted unexpectedly Check whether the character is holding a radio handset.
The radio is completely dead Check the battery in the radio's internal battery slot.
